beats.text: Your phone checks your face with thirty thousand invisible dots.
On an iPhone, Face ID projects more than thirty thousand infrared dots onto your face. You can't see a single one.
An infrared camera reads how those dots land, and builds a 3D map of your face.
That's why a printed photo of you can't open it. A photo is flat. Your face isn't.
A neural network compares that map with the one saved when you set it up.
It also checks that your eyes are open and looking at the screen.
Apple says the chance a random stranger unlocks your phone is less than one in a million.
The old fingerprint sensor? About one in fifty thousand.
The catch: identical twins, and siblings who look very alike, can fool it more often.
And your face map never leaves the phone. It's stored in a secure chip, not sent to Apple.
